In this note we describe the natural coordinatizations of a Delzant space defined as a reduced phase space (symplectic geometry view-point) and give explicit formulas for the coordinate transformations. For each fixed point of the torus action on the Delzant polytope, we have a maximal coordinatization of an open cell in the Delzant space which contains the fixed point. This cell is equal to the domain of definition of one of the natural coordinatizations of the Delzant space as a toric variety (complex algebraic geometry view-point), and we give an explicit formula for the toric variety coordinates in terms of the reduced phase space coordinates. We use considerations in the maximal coordinate neighborhoods to give simple proofs of some of the basic facts about the Delzant space, as a reduced phase space, and as a toric variety. These can be viewed as a first application of the coordinatizations, and serve to make the presentation more self-contained.

outputs.L1:
In this note, we describe the natural coordinatizations of a Delzant space defined as a reduced phase space from the viewpoint of symplectic geometry, and provide explicit formulas for the corresponding coordinate transformations. For each fixed point of the torus action on the Delzant polytope, we obtain a maximal coordinatization of an open cell in the Delzant space containing that fixed point. This cell coincides with the domain of definition of one of the natural coordinatizations of the Delzant space as a toric variety, from the viewpoint of complex algebraic geometry, and we provide an explicit formula for the toric variety coordinates in terms of the reduced phase space coordinates.

Using considerations within these maximal coordinate neighborhoods, we give simple proofs of some basic facts about the Delzant space, both as a reduced phase space and as a toric variety. These may be viewed as a first application of the coordinatizations and serve to make the presentation more self-contained.
outputs.L2: This note examines the standard coordinate systems on a Delzant space when it is realized as a symplectic reduction, and provides explicit expressions for the changes of coordinates between them. For every fixed point of the torus action associated with the Delzant polytope, there is a largest coordinate chart on an open cell of the Delzant space containing that fixed point. This open cell coincides with the domain of one of the natural affine charts arising from the description of the Delzant space as a toric variety in complex algebraic geometry. We also present a direct formula expressing the toric variety coordinates in terms of the coordinates coming from the reduced phase space construction. By working within these maximal coordinate neighborhoods, we obtain elementary proofs of several fundamental properties of the Delzant space, both in its symplectic-reduction interpretation and in its toric-variety interpretation. These arguments illustrate an initial use of the coordinate systems and help make the exposition self-contained.

For every fixed point of the torus action on the Delzant polytope, there is a corresponding maximal coordinate system. The note also shows that each such open cell coincides with the domain of a natural affine coordinate chart on the Delzant space when it is interpreted as a toric variety. Thus, the coordinate neighborhoods obtained from symplectic reduction agree with the standard affine charts arising in toric algebraic geometry.

A central feature of the discussion is the set of explicit formulas connecting the two descriptions. The note writes down the transformations between toric variety coordinates and reduced phase space coordinates, making clear how the symplectic and algebraic constructions describe the same local geometry.

Finally, these maximal coordinate neighborhoods are used to establish basic properties of Delzant spaces from both viewpoints. From the symplectic perspective, they clarify the local structure of the reduced phase space and the behavior of the torus action. From the complex algebraic perspective, they identify the corresponding affine toric charts and help relate the Delzant space to its toric variety structure. In this way, the note provides a concrete bridge between the symplectic and algebraic descriptions of Delzant spaces.

This note examines the natural coordinate systems that arise on Delzant spaces and explains how they are related. Delzant spaces, or compact symplectic toric manifolds, can be described in two standard ways: as symplectic quotients of complex Euclidean space and as smooth toric varieties associated with Delzant polytopes. Each description produces its own preferred local coordinates. From the symplectic reduction point of view, one obtains symplectic coordinate neighborhoods adapted to the moment polytope. From the toric variety point of view, one obtains affine coordinate charts indexed by the torus fixed points, or equivalently by the vertices of the polytope.

The main purpose of the note is to compare these two coordinate descriptions explicitly. Around each fixed point of the torus action, the Delzant polytope determines a collection of primitive edge vectors and corresponding local coordinates. On the symplectic side, these coordinates come from choosing suitable representatives in the quotient construction and expressing the reduced space in terms of moment-map variables and angular variables. On the algebraic side, the same local region is described by a standard affine toric chart associated with a maximal cone in the fan of the toric variety.

The note derives explicit transition formulas between these two systems of coordinates. These formulas show that the maximal symplectic coordinate neighborhood attached to a vertex of the Delzant polytope is precisely the same open set as the affine toric chart attached to the corresponding maximal cone. In particular, the local coordinates obtained by symplectic reduction and those obtained from the toric variety construction differ only by concrete, computable transformations determined by the combinatorial data of the polytope.

This comparison gives a unified view of the local structure of Delzant spaces. It clarifies how the moment-polytope geometry controls both the symplectic and complex-geometric descriptions of the manifold. It also provides direct proofs of several basic structural facts: the torus fixed points correspond to the vertices of the Delzant polytope, the natural affine charts cover the entire space, and the local models near fixed points are standard complex coordinate spaces with torus actions determined by the edge data of the polytope.

Thus, the note bridges the symplectic and toric perspectives on Delzant spaces by making the coordinate identifications completely explicit. The resulting formulas not only describe how to pass from one set of coordinates to the other, but also show that the two constructions encode the same local and global geometry.

**Delzant: For This Moment in Geometry**

Delzant’s theorem is an important result in symplectic geometry, especially in the study of toric manifolds. It creates a beautiful connection between geometry and combinatorics by showing that certain symplectic manifolds can be completely described by special polytopes, now known as **Delzant polytopes**.

For mathematicians, this result is powerful because it turns complicated geometric questions into more visual and combinatorial ones. A Delzant polytope must satisfy specific conditions: it must be simple, rational, and smooth. When these conditions are met, the polytope corresponds uniquely to a compact symplectic toric manifold.

This idea has influenced many areas of modern mathematics, including algebraic geometry, topology, and mathematical physics. Delzant’s work shows how shapes, symmetry, and structure can come together in a precise and elegant way. For this reason, Delzant’s theorem remains a key concept for anyone studying toric geometry or symplectic manifolds.

counterfactuals.output:
We describe natural local coordinate charts on Delzant spaces and relate two standard constructions: symplectic reduction of \(\mathbb C^d\) by a subtorus and the construction of the associated toric variety from the Delzant polytope. Starting from a Delzant polytope \(\Delta\), we show how each vertex determines an affine chart on the reduced space and identify these charts with the usual toric affine charts corresponding to maximal cones in the normal fan of \(\Delta\). Under this identification, the reduced coordinates obtained by choosing a gauge for the torus action agree explicitly with the monomial coordinates arising in the algebraic toric construction.

We also record the transition maps between overlapping vertex charts. If \(v\) and \(w\) are adjacent vertices, the change of coordinates is given by explicit Laurent monomial formulas determined by the integral change-of-basis matrix between the corresponding primitive edge directions, together with the appropriate factors coming from the moment-map level. These formulas make transparent the equivalence between the smooth atlas obtained from symplectic reduction and the algebraic atlas of the toric variety. The note is intended to provide a concrete bridge between the symplectic and algebraic descriptions of Delzant spaces, emphasizing coordinate-level identifications rather than only the abstract equivalence of the resulting spaces.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a paper that develops coordinatizations of Delzant spaces as reduced phase spaces and relates them to toric variety coordinates near fixed points of the torus action.
counterfactuals.output:
The paper studies **Delzant spaces**—compact symplectic toric manifolds associated to Delzant polytopes—and gives explicit coordinate descriptions of them as **symplectic reduced spaces**, then relates these coordinates to the standard local coordinates used in **toric algebraic geometry** near torus fixed points.

The main starting point is Delzant’s construction: given a Delzant polytope  
\[
\Delta \subset \mathfrak t^*
\]
with facets defined by inequalities
\[
\langle \mu, X_j\rangle \ge \lambda_j,\qquad j=1,\dots,d,
\]
one realizes the corresponding symplectic toric manifold as a quotient
\[
M_\Delta \cong \mathbb C^d /\!\!/ N,
\]
where \(N\) is a subtorus of \(T^d\) determined by the normals \(X_j\). The moment map on \(\mathbb C^d\) descends to the moment map on \(M_\Delta\), whose image is \(\Delta\).

The paper develops **explicit coordinatizations** of the reduced space by choosing subsets of the coordinate functions on \(\mathbb C^d\). Near a point of the reduced space, some homogeneous coordinates are nonzero, and one can use the torus action to normalize them. The remaining coordinates then give local coordinates on the quotient. This produces concrete coordinate charts adapted to the faces of the polytope.

A particularly important case is a neighborhood of a **torus fixed point**, corresponding to a vertex \(v\) of the Delzant polytope. At such a vertex, exactly \(n=\dim M_\Delta/2\) facets meet. The paper shows that the coordinates associated to those facets give a local system of complex/symplectic coordinates near the fixed point. In these coordinates, the torus action becomes diagonal, and the moment map has the familiar local form
\[
\mu(z)=v+\sum_{k=1}^n |z_k|^2 \alpha_k
\]
up to conventional constants, where the \(\alpha_k\) are the edge directions dual to the facet normals.

The paper then compares these reduced-space coordinates with the **standard toric variety coordinates**. In algebraic toric geometry, a smooth projective toric variety is covered by affine charts indexed by vertices/maximal cones. Near a fixed point, the affine chart is isomorphic to \(\mathbb C^n\), with monomial coordinates determined by the dual cone. The paper shows that the coordinates obtained from symplectic reduction coincide with these toric affine coordinates, up to the natural identifications dictated by the Delzant data.

Thus, the paper bridges two viewpoints:

1. **Symplectic viewpoint:**  
   Delzant spaces are obtained as reduced phase spaces \(\mathbb C^d /\!\!/ N\), and local coordinates arise by gauge-fixing the \(N\)-action.

2. **Algebraic-geometric viewpoint:**  
   The same spaces are smooth toric varieties covered by affine charts near torus fixed points, with coordinates coming from cones in the fan.

The main contribution is to make the relationship between these coordinate systems explicit. It shows that the local coordinates produced by symplectic reduction are not merely analogous to toric variety coordinates; they match the standard affine toric coordinates near fixed points once the Delzant polytope/fan data are identified correctly. This provides a concrete way to move between Hamiltonian torus geometry, symplectic reduction, and toric algebraic geometry.

counterfactuals.output:
We describe a systematic derivation of coordinate transformations for Delzant spaces from the local integral-affine geometry of their moment polytopes. Starting with a Delzant polytope \(\Delta \subset \mathfrak t^*\), each vertex determines a \(\mathbb Z\)-basis of the integral lattice via the primitive inward normals to the adjacent facets. The corresponding unimodular change of basis identifies a neighborhood of the vertex with the standard positive orthant, and hence the associated symplectic quotient with a standard model \(\mathbb C^n\) equipped with its usual Hamiltonian torus action. On overlaps, the transition maps are induced by elements of \(\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb Z)\ltimes \mathbb R^n\) together with explicit angular transformations; equivalently, they are the action-angle coordinate changes dictated by the integral-affine structure on the polytope.

These coordinates provide a transparent local description of the Delzant manifold \(M_\Delta\). In the interior of \(\Delta\), they reduce to ordinary action-angle coordinates \((x,\theta)\), with symplectic form  
\[
\omega=\sum_{j=1}^n dx_j\wedge d\theta_j .
\]
Near a face, the coordinates split into complex polar coordinates normal to the face and action-angle coordinates along the face. Thus the apparent singularities of action-angle coordinates at the boundary of the polytope are removed by the standard substitutions
\[
z_j=\sqrt{2\ell_j(x)}\,e^{i\theta_j},
\]
where \(\ell_j\) are the defining affine functions of the adjacent facets. The Delzant condition ensures precisely that these local models glue smoothly and without finite quotient singularities.

The resulting coordinate description gives short proofs of several standard facts in symplectic and toric geometry. It immediately identifies the moment-map image with \(\Delta\), describes stabilizer subgroups in terms of the facets containing a point, and shows that the preimage of each open face is a single torus orbit of the appropriate dimension. It also yields the local normal form for Hamiltonian torus actions, the smoothness of the symplectic reduction defining \(M_\Delta\), and the compatibility between the symplectic quotient construction and the associated smooth toric variety. In these coordinates, the usual classification theorem for compact symplectic toric manifolds becomes a statement about gluing standard affine charts by integral-affine transformations. Hence the coordinate transformations not only encode the geometry of Delzant spaces but also furnish elementary, computational proofs of the basic structural theorems of toric symplectic geometry.

counterfactuals.output:
This note studies Delzant spaces from two complementary perspectives: as symplectic reduced phase spaces and as smooth complex toric varieties. The central aim is to make explicit the relationship between these viewpoints, with particular attention to natural coordinate systems and to the affine open cells determined by torus fixed points.

Starting from a Delzant polytope, one obtains a compact symplectic toric manifold by symplectic reduction of a standard complex vector space by a subtorus. This construction gives a concrete description of the space in terms of moment-map equations and quotient coordinates. In this reduced phase space picture, local coordinates arise naturally from choices of nonvanishing homogeneous coordinates, and the moment polytope records the image of the residual Hamiltonian torus action.

On the other hand, the same Delzant data define a smooth projective toric variety. In this algebro-geometric description, the fan dual to the polytope determines affine toric charts, orbit stratifications, and coordinate rings. Each vertex of the polytope corresponds to a torus fixed point, and the associated maximal cone gives an affine open neighborhood isomorphic to complex affine space. These fixed-point charts provide canonical local models for the toric variety and encode the combinatorics of the polytope in their transition functions.

A main theme of the note is that these two descriptions are not merely equivalent abstractly, but are naturally coordinated with one another. The homogeneous coordinates used in the symplectic quotient match the Cox-type coordinates used in the toric variety construction. For each vertex of the Delzant polytope, the corresponding fixed-point open cell can be described both as a reduced chart in the symplectic quotient and as an affine toric chart in the complex variety. The Delzant condition ensures that these charts are smooth and that their coordinates are related by integral unimodular transformations.

The note therefore presents Delzant spaces as objects where symplectic geometry, convex geometry, and complex algebraic geometry meet in a particularly transparent way. The reduced phase space viewpoint highlights moment maps, Hamiltonian torus actions, and quotient constructions, while the complex toric viewpoint highlights affine charts, monomial coordinates, and fixed-point decompositions. By comparing the two, one obtains a unified description of local and global coordinates on the space, together with an explicit understanding of how the fixed-point open cells cover the manifold and reflect the combinatorial structure of the Delzant polytope.
